text: # Competition formats ## Scottish Premiership The Scottish Premiership contains twelve clubs. Each club plays the others three times in the first 33 rounds. The league then splits into a top six and a bottom six based on the standings at that point. After the split, each club plays only the other five clubs in its half once more, giving

plays only the other five clubs in its half once more, giving 38 matches in total. Points carry over across the split, so a team cannot overtake a team in the other half on the final day unless the gap was already small. The bottom club is relegated automatically and the eleventh-placed club enters a play-off against a Championship side.

automatically and the eleventh-placed club enters a play-off against a Championship side. ## Danish Superliga The Danish Superliga uses a similar split system. Twelve clubs play a regular season of 22 rounds, after which the league divides into a championship round of six clubs and a relegation round of six clubs. The championship round determines the title and European qualification

of six clubs. The championship round determines the title and European qualification places, while the relegation round decides which clubs drop to the second tier and which enter play-offs. ## Points and tiebreakers A win is worth three points, a draw one point, and a loss zero. When two clubs finish level on points, the most common tiebreakers are goal

two clubs finish level on points, the most common tiebreakers are goal difference, then goals scored, and then the head-to-head record between the tied clubs. Different competitions order these tiebreakers differently, so the exact rule depends on the league's regulations for that season. ## Promotion and relegation Promotion and relegation link the divisions of a national league system. The lowest-placed

and relegation link the divisions of a national league system. The lowest-placed clubs in a division move down at the end of a season and are replaced by the highest-placed clubs from the division below. Play-offs are often used to decide the final promotion or relegation place between clubs that finished close together in the standings.

# Laws of the Game — selected concepts ## Offside A player is in an offside position if any part of the head, body, or feet is in the opponents' half and nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Being in an offside position is not an offence in itself. A player is

an offside position is not an offence in itself. A player is only penalised if, at the moment the ball is played by a team-mate, they become involved in active play by interfering with play, interfering with an opponent, or gaining an advantage from being in that position. A player level with the second-last opponent or level with the last

A player level with the second-last opponent or level with the last two opponents is not offside. ## Handball It is an offence if a player deliberately touches the ball with their hand or arm, including moving the hand or arm toward the ball. It is also an offence if a player scores directly from their hand or arm, even

offence if a player scores directly from their hand or arm, even accidentally, or makes their body unnaturally bigger by extending the arm above shoulder height. The referee judges the position of the arm relative to the body movement, not merely whether contact happened. ## Video Assistant Referee (VAR) VAR may only intervene in four categories of match-changing decision: goals

(VAR) VAR may only intervene in four categories of match-changing decision: goals and whether an offence occurred in the build-up, penalty decisions, direct red card incidents, and cases of mistaken identity when the referee cautions the wrong player. VAR does not re-referee the match; the threshold for intervention is a clear and obvious error, not a marginal difference of opinion.

is a clear and obvious error, not a marginal difference of opinion. ## Fouls and misconduct A direct free kick is awarded for offences such as kicking, tripping, or pushing an opponent carelessly, recklessly, or with excessive force. A player who denies an obvious goalscoring opportunity through a foul may be sent off. A second caution in the same match
foul may be sent off. A second caution in the same match results in a red card and the team plays the remainder with ten men.
